segments.text: Good morning, good morning, everyone. Welcome back from coffee break. Is everybody with us? Whoo! Are we excited? All right.
Some enthusiasm. Well, hi, everyone. Thank you so much for coming back on time for coffee break and for the active discussions over the past couple of days.
My name is Kadi Touré. I think you've seen me here before. I head global advocacy for the Partnership for Maternal, Newborn, and Child Health.

And me and my co-conspirator, Angela, will be walking you through this session. So we're pleased to have you here. First things first, if you look onto the screen, we have the survey validation QR codes.
So we do ask that you log on and vote, because these will be closing today. So I just wanted to remind you of that. So without further ado, I'm going to take us to our session.
So we've been, over the past two days, working through the different accelerators of the midwifery roadmap. And we've discussed issues related to policy. We've discussed issues related to finance.

We've discussed issues related to education, to deployment. But these have been mostly supply-side issues. So how do we get the midwives to be where they need to be with the resources that they need to have to be able to deliver their services? But today, we're going to shift a little bit to the demand side and focus on the people who are actually at the center of what we've been working on.

So the women and the midwives themselves, and the gap that sometimes arises between the two. So we will have a panel of esteemed colleagues to talk us through some of these. Prior to that, Angela will walk us through a presentation on some of the findings.

We'd like this session, because we're a bit disruptive in the way that we do things, to operate differently. So we will actually be asking the audience questions and getting some engagement from you. In the spirit of a multilingual conference, we will also ask the participants to bring their translation tools, because there are some people on our panel who would like to speak in French.

So we're going to try to force the English speakers today to feel a little uncomfortable to be able to leave the space for the French speakers to express themselves fully. So I'm asking everyone right now to bring their translation tools so that we can move forward. So with that said, I'm going to hand over to Angela to walk us through what I call the Great Divide.
Good morning. Good morning, people. How are we doing? Has someone told you that you look so amazing from up here? Has anyone told you since we came? Let me tell you that you look amazing.
I know a bit of you look homesick, but just know that you look amazing. I feel like I'm doing this for the nth time. My name is Angela Nguku.
I come from across the border. I come from Nairobi, Kenya. I am a midwife by profession turned advocate for mothers and midwives.

I am a natural disruptor because I do not believe in status quo. And as such, I want us, as we are listening to this presentation, to really ask ourselves, I feel like there's something that is missing, but yeah. I want us to talk about the famous White Ribbon Alliance campaign called the What Women Want and Midwives' Voices, Midwives' Demands.

The reason we are here today is because we are talking about something that has been talked about for decades. Midwifery has existed as long as human race has existed. But we are still failing midwives.

And as we fail midwives, we are failing mothers. Unfortunately, or fortunately today, I feel like we are speaking to ourselves. Because the people who are supposed to be listening to us and listening to what we need to do are not here with us.

But at least before we leave here, I would want us to have all of us converted to midwives, advocates, so that we can be able to see what changes when all of us come together as on a shared agenda, not as separate people working on separate issues. Otherwise, why are we here today? Anyway, I talk about what we've heard from Kenya across seven years of listening to over 3.5 million women and girls across the country and more women and girls across Africa, Asia and other parts of the world. We've also listened to over 2,500 midwives in Kenya alone.

Those who know Kenya, when you are trained, you are trained as a nurse midwife. And now at least we are glad to have the midwifery profession having its own pathways and the like. Now, we know, and I've kept on saying this in many sessions, that midwives are the experts of their own practice.

And so are mothers being the experts of their own lives. So it's so unfortunate that for the longest time, when I practiced as a midwife in the different spaces of my work, someone else used to tell me what to do. And every time I speak for myself, I'm told, but you're not supposed to.

And yet, as I was trained as a professional. And I think we are here because we want to change that. And we want to ensure that at the end of the day, the midwives, who unfortunately also are missing here because people, where are the young midwives? We are all aging and getting to the retirement.

And that is a challenge for all of us today. We really need to ensure that at the end of the day, we don't talk about our profession without bringing the intergenerational dialogue about it into the space. So if we really want to see change, we must be willing to let go and let other people come and take over those spaces.
If we are going to retain this profession with this professionalism. Now, one of the things that I've had across board is respect. Mothers have told us that they want to be respected.
And this is not just a Kenyan data. This is data from across the whole world. Women have told us that they want to be called by name.

And now I want you to walk with me. I know some of you on your phones, on your laptops and the like, but I want you to just give me one, two minutes to tell you why it is important that mothers and midwives work together to push the agenda of midwifery. Because once mothers told us they want respect, that is the same thing that midwives have told us.
They want respect. And so they have told us they don't want abuse or humiliation. They want privacy and consent, confidentiality and care without judgment.

That is what respect to them means. Now, they have also told us that they want money in their hand, because money gives you more choices for health. Many people would be like, why would a mother be asking for money? That mother wants to get to the facility to buy medicines, to eat well and provide for her family.

Because as a midwife, I'm told, tell a mother that she needs to eat a nutritious meal. She can't afford it. And for us, what we've realized over time is that a facility means nothing if the journey to that facility is unaffordable.

A closer facility must also work, because at the end of the day, you can't go to a facility and find that there's a midwife working without nothing. So as the mothers are looking for money, midwives also are looking for something else. They want to be supported to deliver that care.

Women want clear health information. They want their choices explained with respect and time to ask questions. But how many of us have given our mothers time to ask questions? Because we are the masters, they are the slaves.

They listen, we talk. And what we are hearing here today is that the midwife models of care dictate that we listen, we partner and have a conversation so that change can happen. Are we willing to relinquish that? And again, I'll pose another question.

How many of us understand really what the midwifery models of care are? Even as we are sitting here and we are saying that we are going to advocate for the same. Women want care that works. Skilled staff, medicines, clean water supplies, privacy and safe referrals.
But how many of us really are giving that? We all know that a mother is more than a maternity case. Anyway, we've converted our mothers to be maternity cases. And that's the truth.

A mother, what I've discovered over the last seven years of working with them, is that she arrives without the realities of her whole life. We see a pregnancy, she sees her whole life. From the time she leaves home, to the time she leaves that facility, to what she has left at home.

She wants money, transport, nutrition, family responsibilities, and the need to be treated with dignity. So for her, quality of care begins long before she reaches the health facility. Midwives have also told us, through the midwife's voices, midwife's demands.

And I'm so happy to see Madam Jemima here because I think she has been a champion of the midwife's voices, midwife's demands. Not just in Ghana, but across different places. Because midwives also, we listen to midwives, and they have told us across board that they also want respect and dignity too.

And I think that's why we are here today. One of the things I've observed over time is that many midwives walk away from their profession with a broken heart, simply looking to survive. Personally, I walked away from practice, but I decided to become an advocate for midwives.
But many people walk away and never go back, because they are frustrated. But we are here because we want to see that changed. Midwives want respectful workplaces.
They want recognition for their expertise. They also want support after difficult births. I am sure most of you are sitting here with mental health issues, because of the things that you observed.

Personally, I tell my story. I was tired of crying at night because of witnessing so many mothers die in childbirth. In the first place that I started my midwifery practice, that was in post-conflict South Sudan.
And I think that changed the trajectory of my life. And I'm sure a lot of us, nobody really thinks about our mental health. And yet, we go through all that.

Mothers also go through the same thing, and we all need the same thing, respect. One of the things that we keep on saying is this, let's not ask midwives to save lives with empty hands. Midwives told us that they want supplies, drugs, gloves, delivery packs, and equipment.
They want space, safe rooms and privacy for dignified care. They want staffing and referral system that is working. But are we giving the same? They also want dignity, respect, fair pay, and a voice.
They want to grow career pathways. They want autonomy. This is one of the hardest things midwives have ever not found in many places.
Scope to practice and care for carers. And a mother's demand is also a midwife's demand. And I want you to work with me in this last slide.
Respect and dignity belong to both the mothers and the midwives. Mothers are asking for respect, dignity, and privacy. Midwives are asking for respect, dignity, and recognition.
Mothers are looking for clear information and choice. Midwives are looking for a voice and autonomy in care. Mothers are asking for medicines and skilled care.
Midwives are asking for supplies and enough colleagues to support their care. Mothers are asking for timely, affordable services. Midwives are asking for fair pay and working referrals.

And I keep saying this, in the work that we are doing with mothers and midwives, trust is the first infrastructure. Because without trust, I don't think we are going to get anywhere. And I am really happy to champion the midwifery models of care.
Because for me, that is where trust has been broken. And that's where trust can be rebuilt. And listening must lead to action.

We've had a cross board over millions and millions of mothers, over millions and millions of midwives. And everyone keeps on saying that we need more midwives. I think we need midwives who are respected and are living and leading lives of dignity.

And the question is, will we listen and ask? And if midwives keep on asking for the same things, and mothers are asking for the same things. The question I'm going to leave you in this room is, what do these two sets of voices tell us? And what will change because we listened? And as such, I want to hand it over back to Kadi. Because unless we really interrogate it together, it will still remain advocacy, accountability is an afterthought.

And I'm here to see in a space where advocacy and accountability is actually the starting point in the first day of any conference. It is again, feeling like an afterthought, being the last day of this meeting. Thank you.
Thank you so much for that, Angela. And I don't think any of us could have said it any better. And thank you for setting us up with the question.

I think what we really want to get to is, who are we providing the services for? And how do they feel when we provide those services? And that should be the starting point for any of the work that we do here. So I want to open up Angela's question, actually, to the audience. In the previous slide, she asked us, have you experienced this? You've seen the disconnect that actually stems from a mirror of each other.

We're seeing the same thing from what women want and what midwives want. So how do we, sorry, I'm trying to get to this last summary slide. How do we get such a gap in communication when both ends of the spectrum want the same thing? And what can we do to help address that question? While you think about this, because we'll take two or three comments from the floor, I want to call up our panel so they can already take their seats.

We'll have a couple of people help us reflect through some of these questions today. I want to call Hawa Abdelaye Elmi from UNFPA Somalia, sorry, who is a midwifery specialist. Martha Adbonyanti, who leads the Mom and Baby Foundation from Cameroon, who we've seen.

Leila Acharay, who's also a specialist midwife from UNFPA, but in Morocco this time. And Sana Omerani from the Ministry of Health in Morocco. While they take their seats, are there any thoughts in the room? We'll have mics run around the room, but what are your thoughts on what we need to do differently and what you heard throughout this presentation? We have one hand here in white.
Angela, would you? Okay. Good morning. Good morning.
Good morning, everyone. Good morning. Judith Awinja from Kenya.
And what I would wish things be done differently. Can we also listen to the men in this room? So that we can get the ideas, also what they need to say. Let them sit there and we hear them.
Thank you. Thank you. Can we have an additional one or two comments before we go to the panel? We have one hand here.
Okay. Hi, everyone. I have one question slash comment.
I don't know, could be either. I was thinking about where the disconnect is, for example. That's a very good question.

And I think that everybody here can agree that there is a disconnect between funding and what women want as well. So as organizations, we have to try and, look at how we can focus on what women want in order to also put that into what we are going to do. And start from what women want by asking them and then use that data to actually plan for activities as organizations.

And as Association of Midwives, for example, a lot of times we try to do that, but then midwives ask us, but what about us? Why are you focusing or leading with what women want? And one way to look at it is, that what women want is midwifery. Women want midwives. It's just the way midwifery is structured nowadays is not what women want.

The way we are organized is not conducive to the needs of women. But we need to restructure and realign what we're doing, who we are, and the professional capacity of midwives into focusing on what women want because midwife is with women. No, that's an absolutely wonderful point and one that we hear a lot in terms of the existing funding structures and what's recognized and what's not recognized.
So a great point. Franca, I think there's a, oh no, we've got five. Okay, we'll take the five and then we'll close and go to the panel because we do wanna hear from our panelists.
Yukari, I'd like to build on the last speaker. I think that as midwives, we've been working not within a midwifery model of care quite a long time. We have to be compassionate with ourselves.

We've been working in quite an interventionist, possibly obstetric model. And because of that, I think we've kind of pulled that into our system. We need to go back to midwifery models of care and also ourselves understand what midwifery models of care truly mean.

And I think many of us don't quite understand because for decades, we've been working in a different system. So I think what we're actually doing now these last few days, this is what we need to do. We need to go back to our roots.
I do think that women want midwives, but sometimes what midwives are doing is no longer midwifery models of care. So I think the answer is getting there. Thank you so much for that.

And I think you heard from the claps in the back of the room that many people completely agree. I will take the two comments on this side of the room because I promised you, and then we'll start with Haua to answer our first question. Good morning.
The microphone is not... Good morning. Oh, hi. Good morning, everyone.
Good morning to this great force of the party. My name is Isaltina. I'm from Mozambique.

I'm a midwife and I'm nine months after I stopped practicing. At Mozambique level, we also trained midwives who did caesarean which was to be able to reduce what is maternal mortality. So I'm a midwife and I also do caesarean operations, as well as laboratories for utopian pregnancy.

But going straight to the question or then reflection of the theme, I wanted to thank or then congratulate me with the points that we ended up or are being taken into consideration every day. To say that for which model, the important thing is that we create a model and this model can leave the role for action. A model, what exists now is a model of care, a model that is focused on the user, a model that is focused on the woman, but this same model, we realize very well that the woman, what she wants is to come and find the midwife to help her, because the woman, she finds someone who has his life in his hands.

The midwife is all that was said, it's not just the one who will be able to assist, but she looks after the family, she is a godmother, she is a lawyer, she is a lot of things, but we end up forgetting ourselves. So we do need this model that looks at the model focused on the user, but we also need to look at this midwife, that she also has a family, she needs to be embraced. What has happened, let's imagine that I'm in a race, there are delivery rooms that are sometimes very crowded, when you leave there, after taking off from the service, if you had a maternal death on that shift, you go home, you are not a mother, you are not a wife, you get there, you are carrying the hospital with you even at home, and the frustration remains at home.

Associated with this, we are having difficulties with the type of infrastructure, we do not have the material, we do not have this defense that a woman, who is the midwife, needs. And I wanted, once again, to say that I am happy to thank this event that is bringing what is the strength that the world needs. Thank you very much.

Thank you so much, thank you so much for that comment, and I think it's interesting that your experience actually aligns extremely well with what we heard from Angela. And what you're calling for is the movement from theory to actual practice of some of the models of care, and some of the recommendations that Franca and Angela raised. So I will take Chair's prerogative to move to the panel.
Please hold your questions, we will get to them at the end of the discussion, but I do, I know, I know. Okay, the last one. I think it's a good communication that she just made.
Generally, in our health system, there are two voices. The voice of the mother and that of the midwife. But the voice of the mother is always preponderant.

We listen to the clients better than the midwives, which even degrades the midwives. The idea would be that the midwife is also listened to so that this right is respected. She needs respect, she needs dignity, she needs recognition.

And to get there, it will be necessary for the midwife to work on herself to have self-confidence. And that's what I appreciate, and rightly so, the training on leadership, so that the midwife knows that she must have self-confidence and work. Another aspect, it will be necessary that since the community already, that we work with the actors of the community, who constitute key actors, to be able to show them the very important role that the midwife plays, both in the community and in taking care of the child, from the community to the level of health training.

So the midwives must work to really value what they do on a daily basis. And the governors must also work with associations to really bring this dignity, this respect to the midwife, and especially recognition. It is necessary to define the recognition mechanisms for the midwives who do their work well.

In our countries, usually, when the midwife hurts, we put it on all social networks. But when she does well, how many times do we put it on social networks? So it is necessary to define recognition mechanisms. Thank you very much.
It's well noted. Thank you very much for this intervention. So Hawa, there's a lot of food for thought on the table.

We've heard some reaffirmations of what Angela highlighted from a midwifery perspective. We've heard from Angela directly about what women want. So where do what women want and what midwives ask for actually meet? What, from your perspective in Somalia, is stopping those needs from being met? And what do we do? How do we resolve this issue? Thank you so much.
And thank you for organizing this important panel discussion. Let me start with very important message. And women are not asking too much.

And midwives also are not asking too much. Both of us are asking the same thing. They are asking a health system that respects quality of life, that respects dignity, that respects women to access or to have their own decision for their reproductive health.

And women, when we listen to the women on GALIS, they demand respectful, compassionate, evidence-based quality of care to be available in everywhere, in every situation. At the same time also, midwives also demanding to access enabling environment, including proper staffing, appropriate remuneration, to be autonomous for their profession. So, these two asks coming from the midwives and the women on the GALIS, is still they meet one very important point, which is accessibility to quality, respectful maternity and midwifery care.

So, we cannot expect women to access respectful quality midwifery care if midwives are not supported adequately, I mean, of working. They are working in an environment that they cannot even access and stabilize any equipment. So, this tells us that our challenge is not simply producing more midwives.

It's about ensuring that midwives are deployed, regulated, equally distributed, and retained where need or where women have the most need that they are expecting. So, I would like to identify key four priority areas that are the most barriers that is obstacle for women and midwives to meet their needs or their asks. The first one, it's inadequate investment and political commitment, because midwifery is recognized at policy level, yet we can also see by experience that there is no domestic financing, despite the government always commits that they support and see midwifery as a priority.
Second is workforce and governance, because there is a gap in regulation. There is also gaps in recruitment and deployment. There is also that gap in data.

And the third is persistent inequalities in access and quality of care, because in the rural communities or displaced communities, adolescents and marginalized communities still often experience limited access to quality midwifery care. And the last one is insufficient community participation. Even though we program and we plan community-based interventions, at the same time, we are still lacking community engagement at the planning stage, especially the key actors in the community, the women, the young people, the community leaders, not only at program implementation, but also at planning stage.

So I would suggest three practical prioritization is to institutionalize community participation, which is very, very important, and also to make midwifery investment concrete for government commitment, not just by committing, but also ensuring that they also commit at domestic financing. And finally, establish community-centered accountability, whereby we use women's feedback and maternity care indicators to measure the impact. So we cannot demand midwifery care from midwives while also they are failing to meet their asks.

And the real measure of our success should not be only to be how many midwives we are having or we are training, but should show how many women also and young girls we are reaching with compassionate and respectful quality care. If I draw an experience from Somalia, most recently we have mapped 10,000 midwives available for the country, and yet 58% are not employed, which is really, that shows that still we have the midwives, but still we are lacking, and that they are also deployed and supported, and also supported not only for working conditions, but also for support of supervision and continuous professional development. Thank you.

Thank you so much for that very comprehensive response, Hawa. And I thought you were very clear about the challenges ranging from political prioritization through to workforce governance inequities. And I'm particularly interested in the question that you raised around insufficient community participation, both at the planning stage and throughout, and some of the examples around community-led accountability.

So we might come to you for that. But Martha, I think building on what Hawa has said, you're a midwife and you founded an organization that works with women and communities, as well as with midwives. So just from your perspective, how is it that two groups that actually want respectful care can land on such opposing views of the debates? But I think to Hawa's last point on the insufficient community participation, how does the system need to change in order to bridge that divide? Thank you so much.

And if I must begin from a very honest note, it's important that we all know that midwives are the best advocates for, or rather women are the best advocates for mothers. Why? Because they are the ones who are the clients. They are the ones who receive the care from the midwives and it's vice versa also.
Midwives are the best advocates for the mothers that they serve. And also midwives and mothers want the same thing. And what's that same thing? It's better outcomes.
They want absolutely better outcomes. Mothers just want themselves and their babies to be fine. And midwives as well also want for their work, for their services to be better recognized.

But most times they end up at opposite sides, mostly because of broken trust on shared realities rather than bad intentions, because most times he may be confused or this midwife is just being wicked. I remember I had an experience one time where we had a community engagement at Pomona Dewey Foundation and I introduced myself as a midwife and one of the women said, oh, you guys are the ones beating us in the hospital. And I had to draw her to the side after I finished my introduction.

I was like, okay, let's have a conversation because obviously I could tell from where I was standing that she obviously has a scar. Maybe she had a terrible experience and probably it's because that midwife too was maybe stressed on her duty. Maybe she had a terribly long shift and the woman just popped in at that time.

So there are different circumstances surrounding that. Also families can feel very displaced because I work particularly in rural and conflict affected regions. Most times the families come in, sometimes they have just one midwife who is on duty, she's been serving for the longest and her tone may not come out as well as she meant it to come out, so it's easily misinterpreted.

And on the other hand, midwives also may feel very stretched. They may be stretched in because most times in facilities there are less tools, less equipment, so they don't get to offer the quality of service that they may in their actual state or capacity as midwives get to provide to those women at that particular point. So women and families need midwives to actually offer clear and respectful communication.

And I say that with emphasis because most times, in fact, always communication is key. You may be offering the best care, but then if you don't communicate it adequately, it just destroys everything. Communication is the basis or the foundation of our work.
If you can't communicate properly as a midwife, it destroys the whole credibility of your work. So it's important that we know that. And also active listening.
These women know when we are listening. They know, they can tell. They can tell when you're focusing or when you just want to dismiss them.

They sense that they are humans too at the end of the day. And midwives, on the other hand, they want recognition. Midwives want, how many of us do not want to be recognized in this room? I want to be recognized.

You want to be recognized. We all want to be recognized for the work that you do because that also gives you a boost professionally to know that you're moving a needle and you're actually helping these women reach an aspect. And also partnership.

Midwives want partnership from these families and communities that they serve. And systemically speaking, we have to stop treating respectful care as just an individual attitude problem because it's not. We have to fix the conditions that surround it.
I'm going to conclude by sharing this voice from the field. It's actually a voice from a mom and a midwife. And I wrote it down because I didn't want to mix my words.
It's 2 a.m. in a rural under-resourced health facility. A woman arrives in an obstructed level after delaying care out of fear of costs and pass-coding. Her family is terrified and defensive.

Inside, the lone midwife has been on duty for 16 hours with no functional referral transport, dwindling basic supplies, and no backup. In her urgency to save two lives, her voice sharpens. To the family, the stress feels like hostility.

Both sides walked through that door wanting the exact same thing, a safe, healthy delivery. Yet systemic neglect has immediately turned allies into adversaries. When we fix the referral pathways, equip the facility, and build community trust before labor begins, that same 2 a.m. moment becomes a partnership instead of a coalition.

Thank you so much. Thank you so much for that, Martha. And so well said that really, honestly, it's because of a lack of fulfillment of the needs of both parties that you end up breaking trust and in a system where two people that should be operating together are not.

And I really like your insistence on respectful communication, on active listening, and on really building a space where there can be that dialogue. And so, Leila, I want to turn to you to see the Moroccan experience. If we have these voices, we have the voices that come from both sides, how do we manage to structure this commitment to convert these voices into a movement and then to generate public demand for what would facilitate a better agreement between the two parties? First of all, thank you.
Thank you for allowing me to speak in French. Of course. It's the turn of the translators.

It's to honor my French-speaking colleagues. So, before answering your question, I would like to remind you that in the room, everyone has the conviction that investing in the profession of a wise woman is investing in life. We are unanimous.
We have heard this saying everywhere. But at this moment, I believe that we need to transform this conviction into a mobilization. Sorry.

We need to transform this conviction into a real collective mobilization to reach the decision-makers who have the power and to achieve sustainable financing. That's the ultimate goal. It's to have sustainable financing for the promotion of the profession of a wise woman.

To answer your question, I would like to insist on four priorities. The first one is the production of data and evidence to convince and to show the benefits when we promote this profession. What benefits do we gain in terms of health, of course, but also in terms of economy and social matters.
But for these data, we should no longer remain classical. We should always talk about maternal mortality. We need to talk about other topics.

I'll give you an example. Why don't we talk about morbidity? It's rare to talk about maternal morbidity that has an impact on the quality of life of women after giving birth or after a pregnancy. It may open the ears of other people and give us a new breath in our pedigree.

The second axis on which I would like to insist is that the pedigree is very important, but we must enrich our classical pedigree into a strategic pedigree based on orientations. It must be targeted and oriented towards results. I take, for example, the example of the Smart Advocacy approach.

I think that FUNIAP is a leader in this approach. There are precise, well-structured tools to lead this kind of Smart Advocacy because it is based on achieving results. The third axis on which I would like to insist is all that is innovation and the use of artificial intelligence.

Using artificial intelligence does not diminish the human capacity in anything, but it is tools that are there, that are available and on which we can base ourselves. Here I can give the example of the Delivery application Safe Delivery application. It is as if we have a teacher or a dozen sound teachers in the pocket of the Smart Woman.

So, it is a support for the Smart Woman in everyday practice. There is also all that is innovation and in innovation it is necessary to work on... It is good to have a good clinical and therapeutic training, but the Smart Woman needs other skills. She needs to learn how to work as a team, emotional intelligence to manage stress.

There are many things that she needs in her training. Of course, it can be achieved either through the system or through associations, but we must be aware of that in order to train a Smart Woman who is able to face all these problems that we have been talking about for three days. There are examples, maybe we will have time to talk about them.

The last axis is always the creation of networks, networks for leadership. Apart from professional associations, we can think of building academic circles that will speak differently about the Smart Woman, build media networks, build parliamentary networks and not always talk about dramas, but also talk about successes, challenges, human stories to attract the attention of decision-makers around this profession. Thank you very much for these very clear axes.

I am interested in the use of artificial intelligence, which is generally a subject that comes up quite often. Do you have a specific example of how it was implemented in your country? I will explain a very simple, innovative example because we are introducing with the schools that train the Smart Women, the nurses too, all the health technicians, a new innovation called Health Attent. Health Attent is an idea competition, it is a competition that we launch at the school level so that the students, the Smart Woman students can learn what a causal tree is, learn that the problems of sexual and reproductive health are not limited to the clinical field, but are linked to sociological aspects, to cultural aspects.

And this Health Attent allows the Smart Woman student to connect with the community to connect with the other options, the other sectors.
